message.content:
**CPU (Central Processing Unit)**  
- **Purpose:** General‑purpose processor designed to handle a wide variety of tasks.  
- **Architecture:** Few cores (typically 2–32) but each core is very powerful, with deep pipelines, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction.  
- **Execution model:** Executes complex, branching instructions one at a time (or a few at a time). Good at serial workloads.  
- **Typical use cases:** Operating system kernels, application logic, database queries, web servers, etc.  
- **Performance metric:** Measured in FLOPS (floating‑point operations per second) but more importantly in clock speed (GHz) and instruction throughput.  

**GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)**  
- **Purpose:** Originally built to accelerate rendering of images and video. Now used for massively parallel workloads (machine learning, scientific simulation, cryptocurrency mining, etc.).  
- **Architecture:** Hundreds to thousands of lightweight cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups. Each core is simpler, with smaller caches and less sophisticated control logic.  
- **Execution model:** Executes the same instruction on many data elements simultaneously. Excellent for data‑parallel tasks where the same operation is applied repeatedly across large arrays.  
- **Typical use cases:** Rendering graphics, deep‑learning inference/training, high‑performance computing (HPC), real‑time physics simulations.  
- **Performance metric:** Often measured in TFLOPS (trillions of floating‑point ops per second) and memory bandwidth (GB/s).  

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| Core count | Low (2–32) | Very high (hundreds–thousands) |
| Core complexity | High | Low |
| Instruction set | Complex, branching | Simple, SIMD |
| Memory hierarchy | Large L1/L2 caches, fast L3 | Smaller caches, high memory bandwidth |
| Workload type | Serial/branching | Parallel, data‑parallel |
| Typical clock speed | 2–5 GHz | 0.5–1.5 GHz (but many cores) |
| Power consumption | Moderate | High (but per‑core power is low) |

**Bottom line:**  
- Use a **CPU** when you need flexibility, low latency, and the ability to handle diverse, branching code.  
- Use a **GPU** when you have a huge amount of data that can be processed in parallel with the same operation, such as rendering pixels or training a neural network.
